science.title: Greenland ice sheet retreat intensifies the African monsoon through a polar-tropical atmospheric teleconnection
science.description: Global climate forcing drives major changes in the North African summer monsoon (NASM), yet how high-latitude cryospheric changes influence tropical hydroclimate through atmospheric dynamics remains unclear. Integrating paleoclimate proxy evidence with coupled climate-model simulations, sensitivity experiments, and idealized atmospheric modeling, we show that Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) retreat acts as a dynamically important amplifier of NASM rainfall. Using the mid-Pliocene as a natural experiment for sustained global warming, we find that NASM rainfall was markedly stronger than that simulated under transient future warming for comparable global-mean temperature increases. GrIS retreat enhances Arctic warming, thereby perturbing the upper-tropospheric westerly jet and triggering a stationary Rossby wave train linking Greenland to North Africa. This polar–tropical atmospheric teleconnection strengthens monsoon circulation and moisture convergence, producing wetter conditions across the Sahara–Sahel. These results reveal a high-latitude pathway through which slow cryospheric changes modulate low-latitude monsoon variability under sustained warming. This study reveals stronger North African summer monsoon rainfall under sustained mid-Pliocene warming than under comparable transient future warming, linked to Greenland Ice Sheet retreat and a polar–tropical atmospheric teleconnection.

science.title: Stayin' alive in marsh muck: The tiny "snorkels" cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
science.description:
Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available. 
Cattails have evolved a solution. Air-filled tubes, called aerenchyma, act like tiny snorkels, carrying oxygen from the above-ground plant down to its roots. 
Some of the oxygen, however, escapes from the roots into the surrounding sediment. That leakage can have important consequences for marsh ecosystems, influencing the microbial communities responsible for carbon cycling and methane emissions in the marsh.

science.title: Environmental impacts and lighting energy use efficiency of hydroponically grown leafy greens under different light intensities and nutrient solution concentrations
science.description: Hydroponic production under artificial LED lighting requires a balance between biomass yield and resource inputs. We evaluated radish, fennel and basil microgreens, and lettuce and basil at baby-leaf and technical-maturity stages, under three photosynthetic photon flux densities (200, 250 and 300 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹; 12 h photoperiod) and three mineral nutrient-solution concentrations (base, 1.5-fold and approximately two-thirds of the base). For the microgreen experiments, biomass and lighting energy use efficiency (LEUE) were analysed using two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD test, whereas treatment differences in DWC-grown lettuce and basil were evaluated descriptively. A restricted life cycle assessment quantified lighting-electricity and macronutrient-fertilizer burdens per kilogram of fresh biomass. Within individual crop–stage experiments, maximum-to-minimum fresh-yield ratios ranged from approximately 1.24 to 2.46, and fresh-weight-based LEUE ratios from 1.72 to 3.89. Radish microgreens grown at 200 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ with a 1.5-fold nutrient-solution concentration had the highest observed fresh-weight-based LEUE and lowest modelled global warming potential (GWP) among the assessed systems. Lettuce and basil at technical maturity had lower GWP per kilogram than at the baby-leaf stage, without establishing lower total burdens per cultivation cycle. The findings indicate treatment-specific productivity–electricity trade-offs under the tested conditions rather than a universal cultivation optimum.

science.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
science.description: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.
